title: GPU clock throttling impact on attention kernel handoffs
content:
Summary:

This is an exploratory runbook + experiment log investigating how dynamic GPU clock scaling (power management, thermal throttling, and clock-domain jumps) affects attention-kernel handoffs and short-tail latency jitter across three kernel families: FlashAttention (Flash), paged-attention (Paged), and fused-op kernels (Fused). Goal is to isolate whether kernel handoff behavior and small-batch latency spikes correlate with GPU frequency transitions and to enumerate mitigations that are practical for Redwood’s serving runtime.

Motivation / background:
- Multiple production incidents where 95th/99th percentile token latency unexpectedly spiked during busy short-burst traffic patterns. Existing traces hinted at kernel handoff events and increased GPU kernel latencies aligned with host-level clock adjustments.
- Hypothesis: transient clock down/up events (driver- or PM-induced) introduce timing variability: kernels launched across different clock domains see different warp occupancy/memory throughput characteristics, causing inconsistent handoff cost when runtime switches kernel variants mid-sequence.

High-level approach:
1) Build microbench harness to synthesize short-sequence, small-batch traffic that stresses handoffs: alternating sequences of caching/warm-up tokens followed by variable-length generation.
2) Run experiments on a controlled node with NVML access to force/observe clock changes: set power capping, simulate thermal event (using stress-ng), toggle persistence mode, and use nvidia-smi --gpu-reset where applicable.
3) Instrument at three layers: CUDA kernel timelines (nvtx + cupti sampling), OS-level power/clock telemetry (NVML polling at 100ms), and runtime scheduler logs (handoff timestamps, kernel variant chosen).
4) Compare three kernel families across identical traffic patterns and two quantization levels (fp16 vs 4-bit emulation) to observe sensitivity.

Experiment matrix:
- Workloads: short burst generation (batch=1..4, seq=8..128), mixed-seq (mix of 8/64/256), steady long generation (warm baseline).
- Kernel families: Flash, Paged, Fused (where available).
- Node states: nominal (no throttling), capped (power cap -10%), induced thermal (fan off / heater on), persistent high clock (nvidia-smi -pm 1 + Xorg disable), and clock-lock (nvidia-smi -lgc to lock ranges).
- Metrics: per-token latency distribution (p50/p90/p95/p99), handoff delta (time between end-of-kernel A and start-of-kernel B), kernel duration variance, GPU SM util, DRAM throughput (sampled), NVML clock frequency timeline.

Key instrumentation notes:
- nvtx ranges wrapped around attention kernel launches and runtime handoffs. CupTI sampling set to 5ms; combine with kernel timestamps in runtime logs for correlation.
- A small shim added to runtime to log: request_id, chosen_kernel, kernel_start_ts, kernel_end_ts, kv_cache_state, batch_id. This is intentionally lightweight (one-line CSV) to avoid perturbing timings.
- OS clock skew accounted for by synchronizing host and GPU timestamps via CUDA event elapsedTime mapping.

Representative findings (preliminary):
1) Correlation between clock ramps and handoff jitter:
   - Clear alignment in several runs: when NVML reports a frequency drop (e.g., memory clock 7000->5000 MHz), subsequent handoff deltas increase by 1.5–3x for Flash kernels in small-batch scenarios.
   - Paged attention shows higher baseline latency but is less sensitive to DRAM clock drops (likely due to algorithmic different locality), so relative jitter change smaller.

2) Kernel duration variance increases near clock transitions:
   - Kernel durations (per-invocation) for Fused ops show multimodal distribution when GPU clocks change mid-run. Hypothesis: register pressure and occupancy interact with clock-dependent bandwidth, causing some warps to stall longer.

3) Handoff cost asymmetric across kernel families:
   - Flash -> Fused handoffs are costlier than Fused -> Flash in many traces. Potential reason: Flash kernels rely on high sustained memory bandwidth and tuned launch parameters; when switching to Fused which may be compute-heavy, the kernel warm-up path and KV cache alignment produce extra stalls.

4) Clock-lock mitigates short-tail spikes but has operational cost:
   - Forcing static clocks (nvidia-smi --lock-gpu-cpu-clocks variant) reduced p99 bursts by ~35% in our small-batch burst tests. However, this increases average power draw and may not be permitted for Dedicated nodes under customer SLAs.

5) Pre-warm / dummy kernels reduce handoff penalties:
   - Submitting a tiny filler kernel (no-op that touches a few pages) on lane transition reduces observed handoff deltas by ~20–40% (depends on variant). Effectively acts as a micro-warmup to get SMs into a consistent state post-clock-change.

Example timeline excerpt (human-readable):
[00:12:23.104] request=abc-12 kernel=Flash start=12031 end=12109
[00:12:23.110] NVML clock change mem 7000->5200
[00:12:23.111] request=abc-13 kernel=Fused start=12110 end=12170  <-- handoff delta jumped 1.8x

Actionable mitigations to try in runtime (ranked):
1) Adaptive pre-warm: when the runtime detects a clock change event or increased kernel latency variance, insert a very short warmup kernel on the target lane before scheduling the first real attention op. Cheap and non-invasive.
2) Handoff-aware batching: prefer to aggregate small requests into a single handoff window when SMs are in an unstable clock phase. Tradeoff with latency tail but reduces degenerate per-request penalty.
3) Clock-awareness policy: surface a telemetry flag to ops teams; if node-level clocks are unstable due to power capping, prefer Paged kernels for critical low-jitter routes.
4) Explicit clock locking as a last resort for Dedicated nodes where power constraints allow; provide an opt-in toggle in node provisioning.
5) Kernel launch parameter smoothing: slightly jitter launch times to avoid synchronized concurrency spikes that exacerbate clock transitions.

Open questions / follow-ups:
- Is the observed behavior driver-specific (NVIDIA Linux driver versions) or hardware generational? Need matrix across Ampere/Blackwell/Hopper(if available) and driver versions.
- For cloud-managed nodes, are there platform hooks (cloud metadata) to request clock persistence? Or will vendors throttle unpredictably?
- Can the scheduler detect clock-change “storms” proactively from telemetry to switch kernel families mid-flow without incurring large handoff cost?

Planned next experiments:
- Run same matrix on two additional node generations (one older Ampere, one new Blackwell) and three driver versions.
- Evaluate warmup-noop sizes to find lowest-cost pre-warm that gives benefit across kernels.
- Implement a quick runtime prototype that: (a) watches NVML for >=2 consecutive 100ms clock delta events, (b) on first new request after event injects a 400us warmup kernel, and (c) measures p99 improvement across 2000 bursts.

Notes to reviewers:
- This doc contains noisy logs; see linked artifacts for full trace bundles (PR 4231 contains experiment harness + trace upload).
- If we move forward with clock-lock as an option, we need SRE/infra input around cost impact and thermal safety.

Immediate action items:
- @Ethan: drop probe runs on an Ampere node with driver 535.65 and upload NVML traces (due 2026-03-12).
- @Marisol: prototype the 400us noop kernel and add opt-in flag in runtime at /ops/kernel_warmup (due 2026-03-17).
- @Liam: validate whether Dedicated provisioning in our cloud images allows nvidia-smi lock operations; if not, document constraints (due 2026-03-15).

Appendix (short):
- Benchmark harness: small-batch generator built on top of our test client; reproducer located in PR link above.
- nvprof/cupti capture instructions: run with CUPTI sampling at 200Hz and NVTX ranges labelled by request id.
- Handy NVML commands used:
  - nvidia-smi --query-gpu=clocks.current.memory,clocks.current.sm --format=csv -lms 100
  - nvidia-smi -pm 1; nvidia-smi -pl <watts>

If helpful I can convert this into a concise runbook for SREs (steps to triage live p99 spikes suspected to be clock-related) and open a follow-up ticket to land the noop warmup patch behind a feature flag.

-- Priya
